reference_calls.source_slice: In 1941 George de Mestral,
a Swiss engineer,
returned from hunting in the Alps with his hound,
an Irish Pointer.
Under a microscope he saw thousands of tiny barbs,
each a hook grasping the small loops in cloth.
In Lyon,
then a weaving centre,
a cotton version proved too frail to survive abrasion.
Working with a textiles firm,
he turned to nylon,
whose hooks were stiff enough to hold yet easy to pull apart.
The name Velcro merged two French words,
velours,
meaning velvet,
and crochet,
meaning hook.
The public was less charmed than expected,
mostly because of the aesthetic.
NASA used it in the Apollo programme to keep gear anchored in weightlessness,
so that nothing would hover in mid-air.
Apollo 11 was equipped with a sizeable amount,
about 3,300 square inches.
When the patent ran out in 1978,
cut-price knock-offs from other countries overran the market,
and a niche product went mainstream.
to stop its brand-name melting into a generic noun,
the company asked people to call such mimics hook and loop fasteners.
In effect,
the firm was asking the public to stop using its own name for rivals' goods.
